newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan should end special income tax cuts - panel.
newsitem.headline: Japan should end special income tax cuts - panel.

text.p: Japan should end its special income tax cuts next calendar year as the economy is on a path to recovery and the cuts could undermine government finances, a government tax panel report said on Wednesday.
"It is not appropriate to implement special income tax cuts," the report said, which includes proposals for reform of the tax system in fiscal 1997/98.
The cuts, worth two trillion yen annually, were introduced in 1994 to spur economic recovery.

If Japan were to continue the cuts, it would have to depend on deficit-financing bonds to pay for them and this could aggravate the critical state of the government's finances and sap the economy's vitality, the report said.

However, the report also added that some panel members think it may be better to continue special income tax cuts if there are fears of an economic slowdown in the fiscal year starting April 1997, and if tight state finances do not allow room for more public works spending to boost the economy.

It also confirmed that the consumption tax increase to five percent from the current three percent should be carried out from April 1997 as planned, which should help prevent state finances from worsening.
The report also urged the central and regional governments to cut spending and tackle fiscal reforms.

On liquor taxes, the panel report recommended that Japan narrow the tax rate differentials between domestic and foreign products, which were ruled unfair by the World Trade Organisation (WTO) last month.

"We must drastically narrow the difference by raising taxes of shochu (domestic spirits) and lowering taxes on products such as whiskey," the report said, adding that a review of liquour taxes was also necessary.
The report advised the government to take measures to help alleviate the economic pain that radical change in the business environment would have on domestic liquor makers and consumers.
The report also said it was desirable for the government to cut corporate tax rates to the level of other nations if there is room to expand the scope of what income is covered.
At the same time, the panel said Japan was in no condition to cut the overall tax burden in light of tight state finances.
Some panel members strongly called for lowering corporate tax rates to help revitalise industry and increase international competitiveness.
Japan's corporate tax rate now stands at 37.5 percent, compared with 35 percent in the United States.

The panel also urged the government to consider a system in which foreigners will continue to be exempt from paying withholding taxes on income gains from bonds issued by Japanese corporations overseas, such as Eurobonds, by devising a way to identify the buyers.
But withholding taxes on such bonds bought by Japanese investors should be paid, in principle, like on those bonds issued at home, the report said.

It also urged the government to consider ways to appropriately assess taxable income amid the deregulation of foreign exchange transactions, taking into account measures taken by other countries in which cross border transactions over certain amounts are reported to tax authorities.
